title: Spaced retrieval (FSRS)
why: Trying to recall something strengthens memory more than rereading it, and spreading recall attempts over time beats cramming. FSRS predicts when you're about to forget each item and schedules it just before then.
caveat: FSRS's advantage is measured as better *prediction* of recall (srs-benchmark), not as proven better learning outcomes than other spacing schedules.

title: Production cards (say it, type it)
why: You get better at what you practise: recalling the Arabic from English builds the ability to speak and write; recognising Arabic only builds recognition. That is the Duolingo trap.
caveat: Productive practice is harder and slower; recognition still helps reading, so listening cards stay in the mix.

title: Words taught inside sentences
why: A sentence teaches grammar, collocation and pronunciation in context and is what you actually need to say.
caveat: Isolated word pairs are learned faster at first; the research is mixed, so the app shows the word alone and in its sentence.

title: Frequency-first vocabulary
why: A few thousand word families cover most of what you read and hear; learning them first gives the fastest gains in comprehension.
caveat: No open Levantine frequency list exists; Levantine order is hand-built and MSA ranks come from a subtitle corpus.

title: Comprehensible input at 95–98% coverage
why: Comprehension rises with the share of words you know; around 95% is a minimum for reasonable understanding and 98% for comfortable reading without a dictionary. The reader shows each text's coverage.
caveat: There is no sharp threshold (comprehension rises gradually), and the claim that input *alone* is enough (Krashen) is debated. Extensive reading benefits are moderate.

title: Speaking every session + shadowing
why: Producing language forces you to notice gaps and automatises what you know. Shadowing (repeating right after a model) mainly trains listening and pronunciation at lower levels. Record-and-compare lets you hear your own errors.
caveat: Shadowing studies are small and mostly with Japanese EFL learners. Self-comparison is not expert feedback; use the conversation session for that.

title: High Variability Phonetic Training
why: Hearing a hard contrast (ص/س, ح/ه, ع/ء) in many words from many voices, choosing, and getting instant feedback reliably improves perception, and modestly improves pronunciation.
caveat: Real HVPT needs many talkers. On iPhone, Arabic has one built-in voice, so variability here is mostly across words; add friends' voices with 'Add a speaker' to make it real HVPT.

title: Short explicit grammar, then practice
why: Explicit instruction followed by practice produces larger gains than implicit exposure alone, especially for adults.
caveat: Effects are larger on controlled tests than on spontaneous speech, so explanations here are short and followed by sentence production.

title: 4/3/2 fluency
why: Telling the same thing three times under a shrinking time limit pushes you to speak faster with material you already know.
caveat: Gains are mainly in speed; the shrinking time limit matters (constant time doesn't help as much).

title: Interleaved review; no semantic sets
why: Mixing item types and grammar points during practice improves long-term retention of grammar. New words are not taught in sets of near-synonyms (all colours at once), which causes interference.
caveat: Interleaving evidence for vocabulary specifically is mixed.

title: Honest metrics, no streaks
why: The app measures learning (words you retain, coverage of real text, minutes you spoke and listened, true retention) rather than app opens. No streaks, XP or guilt.
caveat: This is a design choice, not a research finding.

title: Roots, patterns, radicals, cognates
why: Seeing word structure (Semitic roots, Chinese components, Spanish–Latin cognates) makes new words partly familiar.
caveat: Research on root instruction for L2 Arabic learners specifically is thin.
